action_criteria.rationale: With known frontal atrophy, only the interval change and the supportive features separate a new hydrocephalus from ex-vacuo enlargement.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count, sodium, creatinine, TSH and vitamin B12; HIV non-reactive

action_criteria.rationale: Blood tests do not diagnose iNPH; they only screen for thyroid, B12 or metabolic contributors to the accelerated cognitive decline.

action_criteria.rationale: Her new gait disorder is the target of a shunt, so its baseline TUG and 10-metre walk must be measured before CSF is removed.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Opening pressure 17 cmH2O, normal cells, protein and glucose; 38 mL removed; TUG 38 to 31 s at 24 hours (18%), 10-metre walk 30 to 25 s, MoCA 17 to 18, behaviour unchanged
action_criteria.label: Lumbar tap test with opening pressure
action_criteria.rationale: A normal opening pressure with normal CSF and an objective gait response to CSF removal identifies a shunt-responsive component despite the bvFTD.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 34 s at 2 hours and 31 s at 24 hours (18%), 10-metre walk 25 s (17%), MoCA 18/30, behaviour unchanged
action_criteria.label: Post-tap timed gait reassessment
action_criteria.rationale: Repeating the same timed measures at 2 and 24 hours after CSF removal is what turns the puncture into a tap test.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the new magnetic gait and incontinence to bvFTD progression alone
Do not withhold shunt referral solely because of bvFTD
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 18% in TUG at 24 hours, the interval ventricular enlargement (Evans 0.27 to 0.35) with supportive MRI features and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Counsel that shunting is expected to improve gait, falls and continence more than cognition or behaviour, and that bvFTD continues to need its own management
Discuss goals of care and the expected limited behavioural benefit with the patient and family before surgery
Continue sertraline for the behavioural symptoms of bvFTD
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in a chronic gait and cognitive syndrome without seizures or fluctuating awareness
There is no syncope, palpitation or cardiac question in this gait and cognitive work-up
Echocardiography answers no question in this work-up: there is no cardioembolic event or heart failure
Head CT adds nothing once brain MRI is available, which measures the ventricles, callosal angle and DESH better
Rhythm monitoring has no role without syncope or a suspected arrhythmia
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are
Prion, inflammatory and infectious CSF assays answer no question in a chronic afebrile gait syndrome with normal CSF cells

accepted: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus with concurrent behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia (NPH-bvFTD copathology)

differential.key_features: bvFTD explains the behaviour and executive profile but not the magnetic gait, incontinence, the rise in Evans index from 0.27 to 0.35 with tight high-convexity sulci, or the gait response to CSF removal.

Frontal atrophy widens the frontal sulci, but the high-convexity sulci are tight, the callosal angle is acute (80 degrees) and the ventricles enlarged out of step with the stable atrophy over 16 months.
Falls and a frontal syndrome overlap, but vertical saccades are of normal velocity, there is no supranuclear gaze palsy, rigidity or bradykinesia, and the midbrain is normal in size.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Deep white matter disease is only Fazekas grade 1 without lacunes.
MTA 2 is mild, recall is relatively preserved with cueing benefit, and the cognitive profile is frontal rather than amnestic.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary communicating hydrocephalus (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic)
differential.key_features: No head injury, haemorrhage or meningitis precedes the decline, and MRI shows no haemosiderin.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH requires insidious onset after age 40, at least 3 to 6 months of progression, no antecedent such as trauma, haemorrhage or meningitis, and a gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms [Relkin_2005]

Imaging: Evans index rose from 0.27 to 0.35 over 16 months with tight high-convexity sulci, enlarged Sylvian fissures and a callosal angle of 80 degrees, which frontal atrophy alone does not produce [Nakajima_2021]
Normal opening pressure (17 cmH2O) with normal CSF; TUG improved 18% at 24 hours after a 38 mL tap, above the commonly used 10% criterion [Nakajima_2021]
Tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% with PPV 73% to 100% [Marmarou_2005]

iNPH coexists with neurodegenerative disease more often than chance; copathology lowers the expected benefit of a shunt, mainly for cognition and behaviour, but does not exclude gait benefit [Nakajima_2021]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: bvFTD does not produce a magnetic gait, incontinence or an interval rise in Evans index with tight high-convexity sulci; the tap response shows a treatable iNPH component superimposed on bvFTD.
red_herrings.data_point: Frontotemporal dementia (behavioral variant bvFTD) diagnosed 16 months ago at academic medical center
red_herrings.intended_effect: New gait and urinary symptoms are attributed to bvFTD progression rather than to a treatable hydrocephalus

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Frontal atrophy widens the frontal sulci but does not explain tight high-convexity sulci, an acute callosal angle or a ventricular enlargement that outpaced the stable atrophy.
red_herrings.data_point: Moderate bifrontal greater than anterior temporal cortical atrophy
red_herrings.intended_effect: Ventricular enlargement is dismissed as ex-vacuo change from bvFTD atrophy

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]

patient.history_present_illness: A 73-year-old retired judge with a prior diagnosis of behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD, diagnosed 16 months ago) was referred for a second opinion after her treating neurologist noted a new and accelerating pattern of decline that included gait impairment and urinary incontinence, features atypical for bvFTD. At the time of initial bvFTD diagnosis, she had a 2-year history of personality change (disinhibition, inappropriate social behavior, loss of empathy), executive dysfunction, and mild memory impairment. MRI at that time showed frontal lobe atrophy, with an Evans index of 0.27, and the clinical diagnosis of bvFTD was made. She was started on sertraline with modest behavioral benefit. Over the past eight months, however, she has developed new features: (1) progressive shuffling wide-based gait that was not present at bvFTD diagnosis; (2) urinary incontinence, three accidents per week requiring protective pads; (3) accelerated cognitive decline beyond the expected bvFTD trajectory. Her husband reports that her gait deterioration is the most alarming new feature: she now requires a walker and has had four falls. He notes her walking looks 'frozen'. A repeat MRI obtained six months ago at the referring centre was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available. The referring neurologist asks whether the new gait disorder and incontinence reflect a second, treatable process superimposed on bvFTD or call for a revised diagnosis.

neurological_exam.additional: Behavioral disinhibition evident (tactile/grasp behavior). Frontal lobe release signs prominent: bilateral grasp reflexes, snout, palmomental. No nuchal rigidity.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No papilledema. Full vertical and horizontal eye movements with normal saccade velocity; upgaze range mildly limited for age.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, markedly magnetic shuffling gait with very short steps and freezing on starting and turning; uses a walker. Cannot tandem walk. Pull test: multiple steps backward. Timed gait measures reported separately.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but behaviorally disinhibited (made an inappropriate comment to the nurse). Oriented to person and approximate date. Severe executive dysfunction, minimal insight, perseverative speech, mild anomia. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone and strength. No rigidity. No tremor.
